title: La Llorona (The Weeping Woman)
hook: A weeping woman by the water who drowned her children and now hunts the living.
story:
La Llorona is a Mexican legend of a woman who walks the water’s edge at night, crying for children she killed. In the version told most often, a woman — sometimes called María — marries a man above her station. They have children. She then sees him with another woman, richer and lighter, someone he can take into a world she cannot enter. In rage she takes the children to the river and holds them under until the current keeps them. The moment they go still, she wants them back. She wades in after them. She does not come out the same.

She now walks the banks in white, hair long and black, crying “¡Ay, mis hijos!” If the cry sounds far away, she is close. If it sounds close, she is far. That rule appears in more than one country that borrowed her. Children are told to stay away from the water after dark. Night walkers are told not to follow a weeping woman toward the river. Some tellings say she mistakes living children for her own. Some say she only wants company in the dark. The people who go to comfort her are the ones who do not come home.
mustKeep: Cry is “¡Ay, mis hijos!” Tied to water. 16th-c. omen is a woman wailing before the Conquest — not yet the infanticide romance. Often in white. Do not collapse her into La Malinche.
sensitivity: Infanticide and colonial trauma. Do not mock the cry. Do not present one village’s version as “the” Mexican story. Many regional variants.

title: El Silbón (The Whistler)
hook: A tall plains ghost who killed his father and now hunts drunks; if his whistle sounds far away, he is already beside you.
story:
El Silbón is a figure of the Venezuelan llanos, also told in eastern Colombia. He is heard as a whistle that climbs the scale — do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si — and then falls again. If the whistle sounds close, he is far. If it sounds thin and distant, he is standing in the grass nearby.

In the common origin he was a son who killed his father. A spoiled young man, drunk, demanded deer offal. When the hunt failed, he murdered his father, cut out the entrails, and had his mother cook them. When she understood what was in the pot, the grandfather took over the punishment: the boy was whipped until his back opened, chili or liquor was rubbed into the wounds, a sack of the father’s bones was hung on him, and dogs were set on him. The curse was that he would walk forever.

He is now impossibly tall — some say three meters, some six — a thin shape in a wide hat, a sack over one shoulder. He hunts drunks and womanizers. He sits outside a house and counts bones. If the people inside do not hear the counting, there will be a wake by morning. Dogs, a whip, and chili are said to drive him off. Nothing else is reliable.
mustKeep: Inverse-distance whistle. Origin is parricide + grandfather’s curse (a second variant has the son kill the father after the father abuses the son’s wife — do not merge them). Sack of bones. Prey: drunkards, womanizers. Shared Venezuela/Colombia llanero culture, not “all of South America.”
sensitivity: Graphic family murder. Keep it plains folklore, not a joke about Venezuela.

title: Kuchisake-onna (口裂け女, Slit-Mouthed Woman)
hook: A masked woman who asks if she is pretty, then cuts those who answer wrong.
story:
Kuchisake-onna is a Japanese urban legend that spread in late 1978 and 1979. The figure is a tall woman in a surgical mask, sometimes a red coat, carrying scissors or a knife. She steps out at night and asks if she is pretty.

If the answer is no, she kills. If the answer is yes, she pulls the mask down. The mouth is cut from ear to ear. She asks again: Even like this? No, and the scissors come out. Yes, and she cuts a smile to match hers.

Children invented exits. Call her “average.” Throw bekko-ame hard candy so she stoops to pick it up. Shout “pomade” three times. Say you are late, and in some tellings she bows and lets you pass. Weapons and escapes vary by prefecture.

The rumor moved through juku cram schools, then local papers — Gifu Nichi Nichi Shimbun printed it on 26 January 1979 — then national weeklies, then television. By August the summer holiday broke the gossip chain.
mustKeep: Core script is “Am I pretty?” → reveal → “Even like this?” Modern outbreak: Gifu, late 1978 / first print 26 Jan 1979. Weapons and escapes vary by prefecture. Do not present the “jealous samurai husband” backstory as the Japanese original — later / Western add-on.
sensitivity: Facial disfigurement as monster. Do not imply real surgery patients are this figure.

title: Pontianak / Kuntilanak
hook: A woman who died in childbirth and now hunts from the banana trees, announced by a cry that is quiet when she is near.
story:
The pontianak, also called kuntilanak, is a Malay and Indonesian figure of a woman who died pregnant or in childbirth. Skeat, writing in 1900, distinguished the langsuir (a woman dead in childbirth) from the pontianak (a stillborn child); later tellings fused them. By day she may hide in a banana tree. By night she walks as a beautiful woman in white, hair down her back. The smell of frangipani comes first, then the smell of a corpse.

She announces herself with an infant’s cry or a woman’s laugh. If the sound is faint, she is near; if it is loud, she is far. Dogs howl when she is in the district and whine when she is at the fence. She finds men by the scent of laundry left out overnight. Her nails open them. She is said to take the organs, and to hunt pregnant women and infants.

A nail driven into the nape of the neck — or, in some Indonesian tellings, the crown of the head — pins her. She becomes a quiet, beautiful wife until someone pulls the nail. In 1771, the first sultan of the city that took her name is said to have fired cannons into the jungle until the spirits fled, then built a mosque and a palace on the cleared ground. The city of Pontianak, Indonesia, kept the name.
mustKeep: Modern form is a woman who died pregnant or in childbirth. Skeat (1900) distinguished langsuir (woman dead in childbirth) from pontianak (stillborn child); later tellings fused them — say this on camera. Inverse-volume cry; plumeria then decay; banana trees; nail in the nape. City of Pontianak, Indonesia, named for her; founding legend 1771.
sensitivity: Childbirth death. Do not sexualize her. Living belief, not a costume.

title: Tokoloshe / Tikoloshe / uThikoloshe
country: South Africa (Nguni: Zulu, Xhosa; also Sotho thokolosi)
hook: A short, hairy night spirit that attacks people sleeping on the floor; households raise the bed on bricks to stay above his reach.
story:
The tokoloshe — also tikoloshe, uThikoloshe, or Sotho thokolosi — is a Nguni figure described as small, knee-high or hip-high, hairy, and baboon-faced. Older stories put him in rivers and reeds: a water sprite, mischievous and dangerous, able to vanish if he drinks water or swallows a stone. Later and parallel stories say a witch or a vengeful neighbor can send one. Then he is not only a river thing. He is a weapon.

He comes at night, into the house, to people sleeping on the floor. Illness. Terror. Sometimes death. The household protection is to raise the bed: bricks under each leg, sleep above his reach. Sangomas and certain pastors are asked to drive him out when bricks are not enough.

Missionaries wrote the name down in the 1830s because it was already known; it is documented in English by 1833. The Dictionary of South African English still treats it as living vocabulary. City papers still run the word in headlines.
mustKeep: Nguni water-spirit and/or witch-sent familiar — do not collapse into one origin. Short, hairy, can turn invisible. Protection: elevate the bed. Documented in English by 1833. The “carbon monoxide in rondavels” explanation is modern speculation, not the folk story.
sensitivity: Current belief. Do not call it “ignorant.” Do not lean into older sexualized tellings. Avoid mocking sangomas.

title: Czarna Wołga (The Black Volga)
hook: A black Soviet Volga with white curtains that, in communist Poland, was said to take people after dark.
story:
The Black Volga is a Polish urban legend about a GAZ Volga — the Soviet executive sedan, black as a government car — seen on a street after dark. White wheel rims. White curtains in the windows. Sometimes no plates. Sometimes the number is 666. Children were told that the car takes people.

Who drives it depends on the year the story was heard. Secret police. Organ thieves. Satanists. The Devil, who rolls down the window and asks the time. If the person answers, they die on the spot, or they die at that same hour tomorrow. The counter-charm in the devil version is to say, “It is God’s time.” Then the car is gone.

The Volga was real. Party men rode in them, as did officials who were not questioned. A 1965 Warsaw kidnapping that used a black Volga gave the rumor a news hook. The rest grew as bloc rumors grew: blood sold to rich foreigners, kidneys taken for Soviet clinics. Years later the car in the story changes to a BMW or a Mercedes, but the empty back seat and the white curtains stay.
mustKeep: Black GAZ-21 or GAZ-24; white curtains / white rims. Poland is the best-documented core. Motives shift with politics. Do not use the antisemitic 1968 variant as content. Devil-asks-the-time version: answer “God’s time.”
sensitivity: Child-abduction panic. Skip blood-libel and racist driver variants entirely.
sources: Jan Harold Brunvand, Encyclopedia of Urban Legends

title: Spring-heeled Jack
hook: A fire-breathing figure in Victorian London who used a policeman’s voice to get a door open, then leapt away.
story:
Spring-heeled Jack is the name given to a figure who terrified London in 1838. In January, Lord Mayor Sir John Cowan publicized a letter from Peckham: someone in a devil’s costume was terrifying servant girls for a wager. The papers picked it up. The name was already in the street.

On 19 February, Jane Alsop answered her father’s door in Old Ford. A man claimed to be police and said they had caught Spring-heeled Jack in the lane. She brought a candle. He threw off his cloak. Eyes like red balls of fire. A helmet. Tight white oilskin. He spat blue-white flame and tore her gown with metal claws. Her sister pulled her inside. He was gone.

Nine days later, on 28 February, Lucy Scales walked Green Dragon Alley in Limehouse. A cloaked figure waited in the angle of the passage and put blue flame in her face. She dropped, in fits for hours. He did not touch her. He walked away.

The police never took him. Penny dreadfuls did. For the rest of the century he was said to leap mail coaches, slap sentries at Aldershot, and laugh from rooftops. The last famous claim is Liverpool, 1904. His identity is unknown. The Marquess of Waterford was a period rumor, not a conviction.
mustKeep: Best-documented attacks: Jane Alsop (19 Feb 1838) and Lucy Scales (28 Feb 1838). Traits: cloak, helmet, oilskin, metal claws, blue flame, red eyes, huge leaps. Lord Mayor Sir John Cowan publicized the panic on 9 Jan 1838. Identity unknown; Marquess of Waterford is a period rumor, not a conviction. Do not treat 20th-c. UFO Jack as the 1838 legend.
sensitivity: Core cases are assaults on teenage girls. Tell as historical panic, not titillation.
sources: Mike Dash, “Spring-heeled Jack,” Fortean Studies vol. 3 (1996)

title: Aswang — tell the Manananggal
hook: A village woman who splits at the waist at night and lowers a thread-like tongue into a pregnant house.
story:
Aswang is not one monster. Filipino folklorist Maximo Ramos sorted the word into five kinds: vampire, viscera-sucker, weredog, witch, and ghoul. The image that travels is the viscera-sucker — Tagalog manananggal, “the one who separates.”

By day she is a woman in the village. By night she splits at the waist. The upper body grows wings. The hips and legs stay behind, hidden, because if they are salted or turned over she cannot return. The flying half goes to the house of a pregnant woman, or a sick one, and puts down a tongue like a thread. Through the thatch, through the bamboo floor, into the body. What she wants is the liver, the unborn child, the phlegm of the dying.

Spanish priest Tomas Ortiz wrote a version of this in 1731: the creature on a neighboring roof, tongue like a thread, drawing out the child. Plasencia, in 1589, already listed flying flesh-eaters among the Visayans and called the aswang the spirit people feared most. Counter-charms include garlic, salt, ash, a stingray tail, and light and noise at a wake.
mustKeep: Aswang is an umbrella word — pick manananggal and say you are picking. Self-segmentation at the waist; thread-like tongue. Documented 16th c. Capiz association is popular, not exclusive. Do not retell CIA “Huk aswang” psy-ops as folklore.
sensitivity: Still a living accusation. Do not point at a real town as “monster country.”

title: Banshee (bean sí / bean sídhe)
hook: An Irish death omen who keens for certain families the night before someone dies.
story:
The banshee — Irish bean sí or bean sídhe, “woman of the fairy mound” — is a death omen, not an attacker. She is a woman of the sídhe, the fairy mounds that break the Irish fields. At night she keens. The sound is the sound professional mourners used to make over a corpse, except there is no corpse yet.

She is heard at the old house even if the dying person is in another country. Sometimes she is a washerwoman at a ford. Sometimes a tall thin woman in white or grey, combing her hair on a riverbank. Sometimes an old hag. The cry belongs to certain Gaelic names — Ó and Mac, the families that were here before the Normans — though later tellings let anyone hear her. Once the household admits the cry, death is coming. It cannot be bargained off.

The National Folklore Collection holds schoolchildren’s copies of this: she follows the O’s and the Macs; she is heard the night before; she is not a figure people want to see.
mustKeep: Death omen, not attacker. Irish bean sí = woman of the fairy mound. Traditionally attached to old Gaelic families (Ó / Mac). Appearance varies. Do not import Scottish bean-nighe details as Irish banshee canon.
sensitivity: Keening is a real mourning practice. Not a “Celtic demon.”

title: Bloody Mary (Mary Worth / Mary Whales)
hook: A bathroom-mirror ritual in which saying a name in the dark is said to bring a woman through the glass.
story:
Bloody Mary is an American schoolyard ritual, not a single biography. In a windowless bathroom, lights off, facing a mirror, a name is spoken: Bloody Mary. Three times. Thirteen. Forty-seven. Some say “I believe in Mary Worth.” Some prick a finger first.

If the rite is done right, a woman appears in the mirror. A witch. A girl with a cut forehead. A mother holding a dead baby. She scratches the glass, or the face of the person who called her, or she looks until the lights go back on.

Nobody agrees who she was. Queen Mary I of England is a popular guess that folklorists mostly reject. Other guesses are a witch or a murdered girl. The name slides: Mary Worth, Mary Whales, Mary Jane. Alan Dundes read the rite as puberty fear: blood, a bathroom, a girl’s face arriving in the glass. The story is the ritual itself.
mustKeep: The story is the ritual, not a single biography. Names and counts vary. Scholars do not treat Queen Mary I as the source. Do not invent a “true crime Mary.”
sensitivity: Children’s dare. Do not instruct kids to lock themselves in dark rooms.
sources: Alan Dundes, Bloody Mary in the Mirror (2002)
Jan Harold Brunvand, Encyclopedia of Urban Legends

title: The Greenbrier Ghost
country: United States — Greenbrier County, West Virginia
hook: An 1897 West Virginia murder in which a mother testified that her dead daughter had named the killer, while the autopsy showed a broken neck.
story:
In Greenbrier County, West Virginia, in 1897, Elva Zona Heaster Shue had been married only a short time when she was found dead at home on 23 January. A local doctor first treated it as a natural death.

Her mother, Mary Jane Heaster, went to prosecuting attorney John A. Preston and demanded another look. On 22 February the body was exhumed. Three physicians — Drs. Knapp, Rupert, and Houston McClung — found the neck broken and the windpipe crushed. The Greenbrier Independent reported it that week. Edward Stribbling “Trout” Shue, a blacksmith, was jailed and indicted for murder.

At trial in Lewisburg that June, the State used the autopsy and Shue’s conduct around the body. The defense, hoping to make Mary Jane look unstable, asked her about visions. She testified — the Independent printed the questions — that her daughter had come to her four times while she was awake and said her neck had been “squeezed off at the first joint.” The prosecution had not opened with a ghost. The defense put that story on the record.

In early July 1897 the jury returned first-degree murder after one hour and ten minutes and recommended life in prison. Shue went to the penitentiary at Moundsville and died there on 13 March 1900.
mustKeep: Victim Elva Zona Heaster Shue, died 23 Jan 1897. Autopsy 22 Feb: broken neck, crushed windpipe. Defendant Edward Stribbling “Trout” Shue. First-degree murder, life sentence (Greenbrier Independent, 8 July 1897; jury out 1 hour 10 minutes). Died 13 Mar 1900 at Moundsville — about three years later, not “eight.” The ghost story entered on defense cross-examination, not as prosecution evidence.
sensitivity: Do not say: “Only case in which a ghost convicted a murderer” (tourism copy). Do not invent the “no meat for supper” fight as proven motive.

title: The Phantom of Heilbronn
hook: A sixteen-year German manhunt for a woman whose DNA was at forty crime scenes, later traced to contaminated cotton swabs.
story:
From 1993 into 2009, German police hunted a woman who did not exist. The same female DNA profile turned up at about forty crime scenes — burglaries, thefts, and six killings, including the 25 April 2007 shooting of police officer Michèle Kiesewetter in Heilbronn. Investigators called the unknown woman the Phantom of Heilbronn, or the Woman Without a Face. By January 2009 the reward was 300,000 euros. They released a photofit. It showed a man.

Then the profile appeared where it could not: on papers tied to a dead man. A second test did not find it. In late March 2009, prosecutor Volker Link said the puzzle was solved. The cotton swabs used to lift evidence were sterile — they killed germs — but they were not certified free of human DNA. An unnamed woman who worked at a swab factory in Bavaria had left her own genetic material on unused sticks. Police had been typing the equipment.

There was no female serial killer linking those forty scenes. Kiesewetter’s murder, and other real crimes in the pile, had to be investigated as themselves. The woman whose DNA started the hunt had committed no crime.
mustKeep: Same female DNA at ~40 scenes, 1993–2009. Linked in the file to six murders, including Michèle Kiesewetter, 25 Apr 2007. Reward €300,000 (Jan 2009). March 2009: prosecutor Volker Link — contamination; no phantom offender. Swabs sterile but not DNA-free. Do not name the factory worker. Do not say she “sneezed on the swabs.”
sensitivity: Do not say: One woman committed all forty crimes. Do not collapse Kiesewetter’s real murder into a ghost story.

title: The Brides in the Bath
hook: Three English wives found drowned in rented baths, three inquests that called it accident, and one bigamist hanged in 1915.
story:
In England in the 1910s, three women died in rented bathtubs. Three different inquests called it an accident.

In July 1912, Beatrice “Bessie” Mundy was found drowned at 80 High Street, Herne Bay. Her husband, using the name Henry Williams, had taken her to a doctor for supposed fits. She had made a will in his favor days before. The inquest said misadventure.

In December 1913, Alice Burnham died in a bath at 16 Regent Road, Blackpool, after marrying a man who used the name George Smith. Another accidental drowning.

On 18 December 1914, Margaret Elizabeth Lofty — married the day before under the name John Lloyd — was found dead in a bath at 14 Bismarck Road, Highgate. Another inquest: accident.

Alice’s father, Charles Burnham, saw a newspaper account of the Highgate death and recognized the pattern. Police found one man under the three husbands: George Joseph Smith, a bigamist. He was tried at the Old Bailey from 22 June 1915 for Mundy’s murder. The judge allowed the other two deaths as evidence of a “system.” Pathologist Bernard Spilsbury told the court those tubs were a poor fit for an ordinary epileptic drowning. The jury was out about twenty minutes. Guilty, 1 July 1915. Smith was hanged at Maidstone Prison on 13 August 1915. He was not separately convicted of all three murder counts in that trial.
mustKeep: Killer George Joseph Smith (aliases Henry Williams, John Lloyd). Bessie Mundy, Herne Bay, July 1912. Alice Burnham, Blackpool, 12 Dec 1913. Margaret Lofty, Highgate, 18 Dec 1914. Tried for Mundy’s murder; other deaths admitted as “system.” Guilty 1 July 1915; hanged 13 Aug 1915, Maidstone. He was not separately convicted of all three murder counts in that trial.
sensitivity: Do not: drowning play-by-play, invented whispers at the tub, sexualize the three women.

title: The Shark Arm case
hook: A tiger shark in a Sydney aquarium vomited a tattooed human arm that had been cut off with a knife, opening a 1935 murder case that never produced a conviction.
story:
On Anzac Day, 25 April 1935, at Coogee Aquarium Baths in Sydney, a captive tiger shark, brought in days earlier as a holiday attraction, convulsed in front of spectators and vomited a human left arm into the pool.

The arm had a tattoo of two boxers. It had not been bitten off. Examination said it had been cut with a knife. Fingerprints and the tattoo identified James “Jim” Smith, a former boxer and billiard-saloon keeper, missing since 7 April. The rest of Smith’s body was never found.

A businessman, Reginald Holmes, became important to police. On 20 May he tried to shoot himself in a speedboat and led water police on a chase down Sydney Harbour. On the morning of 12 June — the day the inquest into Smith was to begin — Holmes was found shot dead in his car at Dawes Point.

Patrick Brady was charged with Smith’s murder. The judge directed an acquittal. Brady walked free and died in 1965 still denying it. No one was convicted of killing Smith or Holmes.

Sydney’s coroner, Edward Oram, wrote that it was a million-to-one chance that this one shark, in all the sea, should have been placed in an aquarium.
mustKeep: Aquarium incident 25 Apr 1935 (Anzac Day), Coogee. Victim James Smith; tattoo of two boxers; missing since 7 Apr. Arm severed by a blade, not a bite. Body never recovered. Holmes found shot 12 June 1935, Dawes Point (20 May was his harbour suicide attempt, not his death). Patrick Brady charged and acquitted — do not call him the killer. No conviction for Smith’s death.
sensitivity: Do not: accuse Brady, invent a confession, graphic dismemberment.

title: La Séquestrée de Poitiers (Blanche Monnier)
hook: A woman found locked in her family’s Poitiers house in 1901 after about twenty-five years out of public view, in a case the appeal court would not treat as a crime of standing by.
story:
On 23 May 1901 in Poitiers, France, the prosecutor ordered a search of a respectable townhouse after an anonymous letter said a woman had been locked inside for twenty-five years.

Police found Blanche Monnier, then fifty-two, hidden on an upper floor of her family’s house. She was born 1 March 1849 and had not been seen in public since the mid-1870s. Her mother, Louise, and her brother, Marcel — a former official — had gone on with their lives in the same building.

Louise was arrested and died in prison about two weeks later, around fifteen days after the arrest. Marcel was tried in October 1901. The correctional court in Poitiers convicted him on 11 October and gave him fifteen months, treating his silence as complicity. On 20 November the court of appeal acquitted him. French criminal law then punished acts of violence, not a failure to help. There was no charge on the books that fit standing by.

Early papers, including the New York Times, said she had been hidden over a forbidden engagement. Later court discussion also described long illness in that household. Neither story is a proven single motive. The letter-writer was never identified. Blanche was moved into care and died at the public asylum in Blois in October 1913.
mustKeep: Found 23 May 1901, Poitiers, after an anonymous letter. Blanche Monnier, born 1 March 1849; about 25 years out of public view. Mother Louise died in prison ~15 days after arrest. Marcel convicted 11 Oct 1901 (15 months), acquitted on appeal 20 Nov 1901. Blanche died Oct 1913, asylum at Blois. The “locked up for love of a poor lawyer” line is early press rumor, not a courtroom finding.
sensitivity: Do not: linger on her body, weight, filth, or the 1901 newspaper photo. Do not use “beautiful girl in a dungeon.” Do not invent rats-and-scraps texture.
sources: https://www.nytimes.com/1901/06/09/archives/she-imprisoned-daughter-girl-kept-in-a-dungeon-twentyfive-years.html (coverage fact only, not the sweetheart motive)

title: Dr. Crippen and the wireless manhunt
hook: A 1910 London murder in which wireless telegraphy let Scotland Yard arrest a fleeing couple as their liner approached Quebec.
story:
Cora Crippen, who performed as Belle Elmore, was last seen after a gathering at 39 Hilldrop Crescent, London, on 31 January 1910. Her husband, Hawley Harvey Crippen, an American homeopath, told friends she had gone to America, then that she had died there. His typist, Ethel Le Neve, moved into the house. Friends went to Scotland Yard. Inspector Walter Dew interviewed Crippen. Crippen and Le Neve fled.

Police searched again. In mid-July they found human remains under the cellar floor. Warrants went out. The pair had already boarded the Canadian Pacific liner SS Montrose at Antwerp on 20 July, Le Neve dressed as a boy.

Captain Henry Kendall recognized them and, before the ship steamed out of wireless range, had a Marconi operator telegraph London. Dew crossed on a faster ship, the Laurentic, and was waiting in the St. Lawrence. He arrested them on 31 July 1910 as the Montrose approached Quebec — the first time wireless telegraphy was used to catch a fleeing suspect.

Crippen was tried at the Old Bailey in October, convicted of Cora’s murder after twenty-seven minutes, and hanged at Pentonville on 23 November 1910. Le Neve was acquitted. Later DNA claims about the remains have been disputed; the 1910 verdict was never overturned.
mustKeep: Cora (Belle Elmore) last seen 31 Jan 1910, 39 Hilldrop Crescent. Remains under the cellar, mid-July 1910. Flight: Antwerp, SS Montrose, 20 July; Le Neve in boy’s clothes. Captain Henry Kendall; wireless to London; Inspector Dew on SS Laurentic; arrest 31 July 1910 approaching Quebec. Crippen guilty Oct 1910 (~27 minutes); hanged 23 Nov 1910, Pentonville. Le Neve acquitted. First capture of a fugitive by wireless — not in dispute.
sensitivity: Do not: graphic remains, smear Cora as a “nightmare wife,” invent Dew’s greeting, present later DNA papers as an official exoneration. Famous-case flag: Classic Edwardian case. Use it for the wireless fact, which is unique.
